notable_claims: Locking out users suspected of hacking should be balanced against the user's right to access and due process.
University contractual rights regarding residence hall postings cannot supersede the US Constitution.
Institutions should provide access to 'alt' newsgroups, focusing on regulating inappropriate behavior rather than restricting content.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes several debates regarding the intersection of computing and academic freedom. Key discussions include the ethics of locking out users suspected of account misuse, censorship of physical postings at Iowa State University, and the provision of access to 'alt' newsgroups on university systems.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.46

notable_claims: The institution uses 'crack' to proactively identify and lock out users with weak passwords.
Locking out accounts is mitigated by reinstating them upon presentation of a student ID.
Providing restricted access (compiler/editor without network) for students awaiting due process is technically difficult.
classification.summary: Elizabeth Schwartz describes the practice of locking out users by changing their shells after discovering weak passwords via 'crack'. She argues that immediate lockout is necessary for system security and questions whether due process requires allowing a known cracker continued unrestricted access. She suggests that providing restricted environments for schoolwork would be technically difficult on their network.
classification.title: Article 1--Re: Locking out users

notable_claims: Excessive account lockouts can lead users to share accounts, escalating security risks.
Some universities have permanently barred users from systems as a disciplinary measure.
The right of a user to access university computing resources should be balanced against the collective need for system security.
classification.summary: A discussion between Carl Kadie and David Barr regarding the ethics of locking user accounts during suspected security breaches. Kadie argues that excessive lockouts for authorized university members can escalate problems and may constitute a violation of due process.
classification.title: Article 2--Re: Locking out users

notable_claims: Temporary account disabling is a necessary security response to suspected breaches.
Educational institutions have sensitive databases (personnel, registrar, accounting) that require strict access control.
classification.summary: Valdis Kletnieks argues that system administrators are justified in temporarily disabling user accounts when there is evidence of unauthorized access or hacking. He distinguishes between temporary security lockdowns and permanent bans, suggesting the former is a necessary preventative measure regardless of whether all hacking is inherently dangerous.
classification.title: Article 3--Re: Locking out users

notable_claims: Lockouts in academic environments are only justified if accounts are compromised, less drastic communication fails, serious offenses continue, or due process has been followed.
Some university computer policies provide a false illusion of due process while granting expansive discretion for harsh punishment.
Certain institutional policies may violate federal FERPA regulations by allowing the seizure of user files.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the ethical and procedural requirements for locking users out of academic computer systems, arguing that such actions should generally follow due process. He provides a series of critiques regarding university computer policies that lack transparency or fair appeal processes. The post highlights specific institutional failures in protecting user rights across several universities.
classification.title: Article 4--Due process when Locking out users

identity.subject: Article 4--Due process when Locking out users

notable_claims: Iowa State University implemented a policy on August 16, 1992, prohibiting materials in student room corridors.
Violations of the posting policy could result in the termination of student housing contracts.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding a new policy at Iowa State University prohibiting the posting of materials on the exterior of student rooms. The policy warns that 'creative' methods to circumvent these rules will be handled contractually, potentially leading to termination of housing contracts.
classification.title: Censorship at Iowa State

notable_claims: The absence of viewpoint discrimination is not evidence of the absence of censorship.
Contractual rights of a state university cannot supersede the US Constitution.
classification.summary: J. S. Greenfield argues against a university policy restricting 'door art' and postings in residence halls at Iowa State University. He contends that uniform application of a restrictive rule does not negate censorship and that state universities cannot use contractual agreements to supersede First Amendment rights.
classification.title: Re: Censorship at Iowa State

notable_claims: Public university administrations are subject to government free speech restrictions.
Banning all expression in a public area is still a form of censorship, even if it is not viewpoint discrimination.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the legality of Iowa State University's restrictions on posting materials on dormitory doors. The author argues that as a public institution, the university administration acts as the government and cannot arbitrarily restrict free expression in public areas. The debate centers on whether such policies constitute censorship or legitimate 'time, place and manner' restrictions.
classification.title: Re: Censorship at Iowa State

notable_claims: Dartmouth Computing Services decided not to engage in the 'censorship business' regarding student printing.
Decisions on newsgroup feeds at Dartmouth were primarily departmental rather than university-wide.
classification.summary: Geoff Bronner discusses Dartmouth's policy of receiving all newsgroups, including the alt.* hierarchy. He notes that while Computing Services makes these decisions, they have historically avoided censorship, even when students printed questionable material. Bronner argues that if a site can afford the feed, it should allow full access to avoid restricting content.
classification.title: Article 8--Re: What do you do about alt.*

identity.subject: Article 8--Re: What do you do about alt.*

notable_claims: Suggests that offensive content should be managed via public behavior policies rather than restricting private access or storage.
classification.summary: Marshall G. Flax responds to a query regarding the management of the 'alt' newsgroup hierarchy and offensive imagery at universities. He argues against restricting private reading or storage, suggesting instead that policies focus on public behavior and printing restrictions. He notes that Princeton University employs a similar policy.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: What do you do about alt.*

identity.subject: Article 9--Re: What do you do about alt.*

notable_claims: Academic freedom is an essential pre-condition for the functions of higher education institutions.
Institutions of higher education should strive to prevent scientific and technological dependence.
Universities have an obligation to prevent the misuse of science and technology to the detriment of human rights.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares the 'Lima Declaration on Academic Freedom and Autonomy of Institutions of Higher Education,' adopted by the World University Service in 1988. The document defines academic freedom as the right of the academic community to pursue and transmit knowledge without interference or repression. It emphasizes institutional autonomy from state control and the responsibility of universities to prevent the misuse of science and technology.
classification.title: World University Service's Academic Freedom declaration
